Chapter 4

Blockchain-Based Technologies as an Opportunity for Enhanced Access Control

  • Hugo Santos Martins
    University of Lisbon, Portugal
  • Sérgio Guerreiro
    University of Lisbon, Portugal

ABSTRACT

There is an increasing gap between the needs of modern, complex, and distributed environments in regards to control of access to data and the level to which classical access control solutions can fulfill those needs. The purpose of this chapter is to highlight the current state of art of existing research over access control in increasingly decentralized environments and to argue how the subject of access control is more relevant than ever before, with increasing research opportunities emerging. In this chapter, the authors analyze the current state of the art of access control mechanisms and systems over decentralized applications with a focus on enterprise ecosystems, analyze the current challenges and opportunities that the new technological landscape offers, specifically over the application of blockchain-based technologies in access control, and propose new research directions for the future.

INTRODUCTION

Access control has been a subject of research since the early inceptions of the digital era, from time-sharing systems such as the ADEPT-50 (Weissman, 1969) research conducted in the 1970s (Graham & Denning, 1972; Bell & LaPadula, 1973; Lampson, 1974), cloud computing (Yu, Wang, Ren, & Lou, 2010; Wang, Liu, & Wu, 2010; Wan, Liu, & Deng, 2012; Ruj, Nayak, & Stojmenovic, 2011) and, more recently, over the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem (Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, & Ait Ouahman, 2017; Dorri, Kanhere, & Jurdak, 2016). Nonetheless, it is a subject with endless research opportunities due to the continuous advances offered in the industry.

Although it has been deeply researched, there is an increased perception of its importance due to, among other things, recent and recurring data breaches (Burgess, 2017; Lieber, 2017; The Guardian, n.d.), and the rise of IoT devices’ usage and cloud services. Increasingly complex and distributed technological ecosystems, with increasing numbers of users, demand different approaches to the subject of access control and its management. With information and resources increasingly scattered around the globe, in high-functioning distributed clusters of computational capacity, new challenges to the current access control methodologies are emerging. In an increasingly digital world, in which huge quantities of data are created each day, it is becoming a necessity to strengthen and adapt the mechanisms of access control.

A survey over existing decentralized access control solutions (Miltchev, Smith, Prevelakis, Keromytis, & Ioannidis, 2008) for distributed file systems has found issues with ease of use, scalability, and management difficulties, especially over permission revocation. Existing access control solutions for cloud services are either centralized (Calero, Edwards, Kirschnick, Wilcock, & Wray, 2010; Ruj, Nayak, & Stojmenovic, 2011; Yu, Wang, Ren, & Lou, 2010) or rely heavily on complex Public Key Infrastructure and Key Distribution Centers (Ruj, Stojmenovic, & Nayak, 2012; Ruj, Stojmenovic, & Nayak, 2014; Bauer, Garriss, & Reiter, 2005). A review of the state of art over access control in IoT (Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, & Ait Ouahman, 2017) has suggested a modern approach to access control should be concerned with providing ”many and diverse approaches” (p. 242) rather than a ”one-size-fits-all approach” (p. 242).

Ouaddah, Mousannif, Elkalam, and Ouahman (2017) suggest that current IoT access control solutions face two main challenges: developing improved access control mechanisms over the classical ones, and developing decentralized approaches to access control in IoT in an effort to improve security and ensure privacy. Access control for the Internet has also been researched by using smart certificates over a centralized architecture (Park & Sandhu, 1999).

Other efforts in researching decentralized access control are either outdated for modern applications (Satyanarayanan, 1989; Karger, 1977) or are purely theoretical (Thomas & Sandhu, 1993). Much of the existing research has been found to be centralized, lacking in implementations, for current systems, lacking in scalability capacities and traceability, focused on IoT or cloud services.

The previous two paragraphs are meant to expose how, even though access control has previously been researched extensively, the industry has continuously posed new challenges to the very concept and mechanisms of access control, as well as its implementations. This chapter aims to analyze and expose the current state of art in access control, over complex and highly distributed, and increasingly decentralized, technological ecosystems, the challenges posed by these new environments and the new research opportunities that are emerging. It is important that a boundary be set between decentralized and distributed applications. This will allow a deeper understanding of the concepts brought forth by this chapter.

In that sense, a distributed system is one that is distributed, geographically, physically or virtually, but may still maintain centralized authority elements, whereas a decentralized system is one that does not possess a centralized authority element, and in which each element is an authority in itself, coordinating the status of the entire system by communicating with other elements, through consensus protocols (Castro & Liskov, 1999). In this context, a decentralized systems is inherently distributed but a distributed system is not necessarily decentralized.

This chapter begins with an analysis over the current state of art in access control systems, with a focus on decentralized and distributed ecosystems, as well as a short introduction to existing blockchain literature. Although risks exist for businesses, technological innovation brings along new challenges and a potential for opportunities that business could take advantage of. Furthermore, this chapter also covers the technical challenges and risks, concerning access control, that will have to be faced globally, by the rise of number of attacks and attack vectors, increasingly complex and decentralized ecosystems, technology innovation and the shortage of labor for access control systems and solutions.

The authors also discuss the potential and innovation of new technology, such as blockchain technology in the enhancement of access control systems, and access control in businesses globally that will certainly set a turning point in how access control is managed, audited and secured – as well as how those new advances can be used by businesses to improve their operations.

As a prime example, blockchain-based technologies (Nakamoto, 2008; Buterin, 2013; Wood, 2014) and services – a disruptive technological innovation – offer exciting new perspectives, both for individuals and organizations in terms of enhanced security and decentralization, in industries as diverse as health-care, public administration or financial services. Although there is an increased global perception of blockchain-related technologies’ potential, there remains a shortage of professional knowledge. This shortage undermines the potential transformation, of this disruptive technological innovation, into practical applications, that are able to mitigate security and business risks, created by today’s technological landscape, that are becoming increasingly demanding.

In conclusion, this chapter’s objectives are threefold. The authors intend to analyze the current state-of-art of access control mechanisms and systems over decentralized applications, analyze the current challenges and opportunities that the new technological landscape offers in this field, and, finally, propose new research directions for future research.

BACKGROUND

The purpose of this chapter is to present a review of the existing literature in the research fields of Access Control and Blockchain. At the same time, we want to contextualize our problem statement within the existing academic literature. It is important that, through this review, the knowledge already established in Access Control, as well as its qualities and weaknesses, becomes clearer. A review of blockchain technology is also presented, the latter section, to establish the existing literature, use cases and potential of this technology.

Access Control

Access Control has been a thoroughly studied research field. Since the late 1950s and early 1960s – initially for military purposes – Access Control has been studied with all sorts of methodologies - from theoretical approaches to implementation-based research. After the initial military-focused research, Access Control started being researched even deeper for applications and solutions for commercial enterprises throughout the 1970s and 1980s. With the emergence of the Internet, new and exciting possibilities emerged as well, along with new challenges in Access Control. Today Access Control still faces challenges and new opportunities in increasingly broader areas due to the pervasiveness of technology in almost all areas of society.

From the dawn of the computer age through the Internet boom to the digital transformation era, control of access either physical or digital has been a key component of technology. The academic literature available is very broad, from centralized to decentralized systems, diverse access control models and different approaches to the subject of access control and trust management. This section intends to shed light on the current state of the art of the field of Access Control, in particular with regards to this chapter’s objects.

Discretionary Access Control

One of the foundational access control approaches is Discretionary Access Control (DAC), which is an approach characterized by allowing access control policies to be defined dynamically for subjects and resources. In most DAC models only two elements are identified: subjects and objects. With DAC, policy enforcement is achieved by comparing a subject and its associated groups with the resources’ group permissions. In other words, validation is performed to answer the following question: is the subject, or a group the subject belongs to, allowed access to a specific resource? Biba’s definition of discretionary access control (Biba, 1977), or integrity policy, as it was known at the time, states:

(..), a discretionary policy is one in which the protection may be dynamically (during the existence of an object) defined by the user. (p. 23)

Research developed to date has focused on analyzing the current existing access control models. Access Control Lists (ACLs) are one of the foundational models for implementing access control policies and rely on lists with defined subjects that are allowed access to specific objects. From those lists, policy enforcement can be dynamically achieved by looking up information contained inside the list whenever access to an object is requested. Along with ACLs is another relevant conceptual model referred to as the Access Matrix. Graham and Denning (1972) and Lampson (1974) developed early research on this model, and was further developed by Harrison, Ruzzo, and Ullman (1976).

Access matrices are defined by a matrix composed of both objects and subjects – subjects which can be replaced by access domains or groups – that define a system’s access control policy. During policy enforcement, access to an object is allowed if the intersection between subject and object bears a policy that allows access to said object. Different implementations of access matrices can be found (Graham & Denning, 1972; Lampson, 1974; Harrison, Ruzzo, & Ullman, 1976), with Harrison, Ruzzo, and Ullman (1976) being known as the Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman (HRU) model.

Lastly, another relevant model was proposed, more than a decade later (Sandhu, 1992). Representing an evolution from the HRU model, the Typed Access Matrix (Sandhu, 1992) was intended to provide a broader application to the concept of access matrices. HRU’s definition had a set of undecidable cases when performing policy enforcement, which left it vulnerable as an access control model. Sandhu (1992) noted that, ”[m]ost security policies of practical interest fall into the undecidable cases of HRU” (p. 122) which prompted the development of TAM. TAM was based on previous research (Sandhu, 1988; Sandhu, 1992) and was safer and allowed more expressiveness than previous research (Harrison, Ruzzo, & Ullman, 1976).

Early implementations of discretionary access control can be found in systems such as MULTICS (Organick, 1972) and ADEPT-50 (Weissman, 1969) which featured more specific contexts and implementations.

Mandatory Access Control

On another research direction, Denning (1976) suggest a mathematical model for secure information flow based on the concept of a lattice whose purpose is to guarantee security in the transmission of information between systems. A lattice allows for the definition of classes bound to objects and subjects. Using only this, it is effectively possible to define an access control policy in a specific system. These security classes, defined and then bound separately for objects and subjects, allow for the necessary validations in the moment of policy enforcement.

Policy enforcement in a lattice-based model is performed by comparing the security class associated with a subject with the security class of an object – allowing access only if the subject’s security class allows it to access said object. This research, originally developed for military applications, can be best understood if we consider the concept of military clearances. A subject is only allowed access to an object if its clearance allows him to access said object. Denning (1976) served as the formal definition of an initial Lattice-based Access Control that would later be improved and explained (Sandhu, 1993).

In the same research, the impact if Lattice-based Access Control is described as:

At the same time it must be appreciated that the lattice-based approach does not provide a complete solution for information flow policies, let alone for security policies in general. In other words the lattice-based approach is but one ingredient of computer security, albeit a very important one. (p. 19)

This helps to understand the volatility of access control models and solutions. With new technology and new systems, new access control challenges emerge. Lattice-based Access Control is only one of a number of access control models that are part of an access control approach defined as Mandatory Access Control (MAC). MAC can be be defined by an approach to access control that embeds access control policy, inside systems rather than in external sources. This approaches differs from DAC by being less flexible and more secured in most implementations, and inherently static. Nonetheless, like DAC, MAC relies on two elements – subjects and objects – with an extension of the security classes to be associated with each. Early research over MAC was also conducted with a focus on military applications. Biba (1977) defines mandatory integrity policy as:

(...) a protection policy which, once defined for an object, is unchangeable and must be satisfied for all states of the system (as long as the object exists). (p. 23)

Relevant models for MAC, apart from Denning (1976), also further explained and analyzed by Sandhu (1993), are the Bell-LaPadula (Bell & LaPadula, 1973), formally defined before Denning (1976) and the Biba models (Biba, 1977). Sandhu (1993) started to study access control from a commercial perspective rather than from a purely military one, specifically for lattice-based access control.

Role-Based Access Control

With increasing demand for commercial solutions in access control, new approaches started to emerge. Ferraiolo and Kuhn (1992) conducted research that developed a new model for access control – Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) – which represented a considerable evolution over the existing MAC and DAC models which were previously analyzed. RBAC introduced the concept of roles as an intermediary abstraction between the object and subjects, in access control. With RBAC, policy definition was composed of three elements: subjects, objects, and roles. In this sense, RBAC is already different from the solutions as described above. With RBAC, roles are defined as a function of, for example, employee’s job titles. Each subject is assigned a role and each object is allowed access to a set of roles. During policy enforcement, the validation performed is if the subject is a member of the defined roles to which the object allows access.

RBAC made policy management easier and it was better suited for application systems that were commercially-focused instead of the military-based applications for which access control had been developed. The reason for this suitability is due to the manner in which organizations are usually structured. Organizations, unlike the military, have employees assigned specific business roles and functions. Those roles carry with them a set of tasks and permissions that every employee, assigned to that role, must possess. Organizations can easily have dozens, hundreds or thousands of employees which makes managing policy at an individual level, painstakingly difficult. By abstracting individual employees into sets of roles, the set of definitions that are needed decreases dramatically.

Initially presented as part of the MAC approach to access control, RBAC quickly spread not only as a model but rather as an entirely new approach to access control. Sandhu, Coyne, Feinstein, and Youman (1996) present an analysis of the previous definitions of RBAC, presenting a family of RBAC reference models, commonly named RBAC96 – effectively consolidating a new approach to access control. This research presents as an evolution of the initial RBAC definition (Ferraiolo & Kuhn, 1992) by adding the concept of role hierarchies and constraints to it.

The beginning RBAC reference models presented by Sandhu, Coyne, Feinstein, and Youman (1996) included the following:

  • • RBAC0: Base RBAC.
  • • RBAC1: RBAC0 + Role Hierarchy.
  • • RBAC2: RBAC0 + Constraints.
  • • RBAC3: RBAC1 + RBAC2.

Analysis and enhancement of the RBAC models and approach has continuously been produced ever since RBAC was first introduced, generating a wide array of RBAC variations concerning broader aspects of commercial applications. Research covering the addition of temporal constraints into RBAC was produced in Bertino, Bettini, Ferrari, and Samarati (1998), and Bertino, Bettini, Ferrari, and Samarati (1996). A more formal model was latter defined as Temporal Role-based Access Control (TRAC) (Bertino, Bonatti, & Ferrari, 2000). Bonatti, Galdi, and Torres (2013) presented the Enterprise Role-based Access Control (ERBAC) . Covington, Moyer, and Ahamad (2000) offered an interesting concept that evolves the RBAC model – Generalized Role-based Access Control (GRBAC) – by adding the concepts of role typification.

Team-based Access Control (TMAC) (Thomas, 1997) was presented as an expression of Role-based Access Control in collaborative environments. Ray, Kumar, and Yu (2006) introduced yet another variant of the RBAC model, Location-aware Role-based Access Control (LRBAC), which stands for introducing the use of location data to increase system security and access control. This model evolves from earlier research (Damiani, Bertino, Catania, & Perlasca, 2007) with GEO-RBAC.

Osborn, Sandhu, and Munawer (2000) demonstrated how the constructs created by RBAC can be applied in systems that use MAC or DAC. The relevance of this research is that a transformation can be applied to update legacy DAC, or MAC, configurations into RBAC-based access control, effectively guaranteeing that RBAC can be used as a MAC or DAC.

Attribute-Based Access Control

Apart from DAC, MAC and RBAC, another relevant approach to access control exists which is Attribute-based Access Control (ABAC). In ABAC, different from what has been described above in the other approaches, access control is provided by containing a specific element, apart from subjects, objects and roles – attributes. ABAC utilizes subject and object attributes (or environment attributes) in policy definition as well as in policy enforcement. The usage of attributes, in access control policy definition and enforcement, increases the expressiveness of policies and allows policy enforcement to be based more on dynamic data - increasing the effectiveness of access control.

Recently, Hu et al. (2014) presented a guide with the purpose of unifying the definition of ABAC and analyzing some considerations of ABAC implementations in organizations. In this research, some of the ABAC benefits are defined as the following:

  • • ABAC avoids assigning authorizations to subjects explicitly, easing the burden of access control management.
  • • More flexibility for usage in complex environments, where ACLs or RBAC would be too complex and difficult to manage.
  • • Fine-grained access control that considers attributes from several different inputs.

ABAC was also the subject of research in Wang, Wijesekera, and Jajodia (2004), Cruz, Gjomemo, Lin, and Orsini (2008) and Yuan & Tong (2005), proposing several informal definitions for ABAC. In Hu et al. (2014), ABAC is defined as follows:

An access control method where subject requests to perform operations on objects are granted or denied based on assigned attributes of the subject, assigned attributes of the object, environment conditions, and a set of policies that are specified in terms of those attributes and conditions. (p. 7)

A mature ABAC model doesn not exist yet like the models presented for DAC, MAC, and RBAC. Nonetheless, Jin, Krishnan, and Sandhu (2012) tried to overcome this challenge by presenting a ”unified” ABAC model capable of covering access control implementations of DAC, MAC, and RBAC. By doing this, they have effectively established that ABAC is an approach capable for emerging technologies and environments and, simultaneously, that it can also be used in legacy implementations needing enhanced capabilities and fine-grained solutions. Nonetheless, other research has been conducted regarding this approach (Zhang, Li, & Nalla, 2005), and a model was proposed for the enhancement of the access matrix model, described in earlier sections, with attribute capabilities.

Distributed Access Control

The study of access control in distributed systems has spanned several decades since the early developments of distributed systems through grid and cloud computing and cloud systems. Some of the beginning studies developed in the field of access control in decentralized environments (Karger, 1977) encompass much of the knowledge to date. As with initial research regarding access control models, Karger (1977) presents the challenges in distributed systems when applying MAC to a decentralized system. It recognizes that not all algorithms that guarantee access control in centralized systems can be easily mapped to a decentralized system, thus presenting a new way to work with lattice-based access control models that can be used in decentralized systems.

Moffett, Sloman, and Twidle (1990) proposed a specification for the implementation of discretionary access control in distributed systems. In this research, the concept of domains, groups of objects and access rules were introduced as a way of helping structure the way access control is managed in a highly distributed and complex system. This work evolved, in part, from Satyanarayanan (1989) on security in complex distributed systems. Research over the Andrew system (Satyanarayanan, 1989), explored how to introduce access control in complex distributed systems. Sandhu and Suri (1992), presented enhancements over Sandhu’s initial Typed Access Matrix model (Sandhu, 1992). This research proposed a simpler TAM, called SO-TAM, that made it easier to implement Typed Access Matrix, in distributed environments, as well as demonstrated the usage of digital certificates in access Control.

Johnston, Mudumbai, and Thompson (1998) present a mechanism for access control in distributed systems. The system described leverages the research and capacity of digital certificates to allow access control in distributed systems. This research represents the evolution in the area of access control in distributed systems and revalidates its relevance. Sandhu and Park (1998) present the decentralization of access control management in RBAC models, in web-based systems. This research presents a way to try and decentralize the management of access control, but it still does not decentralize the policy engine behind the access control. Sandhu and Park (1998) was an enhancement over a previous specification (Barkley, Cincotta, Ferraiolo, Gavrila, & Kuhn, 1997). The research presented (Sandhu & Park, 1998) was evolved through the use of X.509 certificates (Park & Sandhu, 1999) and Park, Sandhu, and Ahn (2001) return to examine this research.

Harrington and Jensen (2003) note that one of the main problems in the area of access control is the centralization of the reference monitors, and present a proposal for a cryptographic access control system, which is inherently distributed but not completely decentralized. This research evolves what has been presented earlier (Satyanarayanan, 1989). Park and Hwang (2003) demonstrate the application of the RBAC model in peer-to-peer environments, which is an evolution towards a more complete decentralization of access control. Abiteboul et al. (2004) present the implementation of a distributed system of access to confidential patient data, in a distributed way, through XML data that presents an evolution over the research produced earlier (Damiani, De Capitani di Vimercati, Paraboschi, & Samarati, 2002).

Bhatti, Shafiq, Bertino, Ghafoor, and Joshi (2005) present a system - X-GTRBAC - for access control management, in GTRBAC model (Joshi, Bertino, Latif, & Ghafoor, 2005), over decentralized environments. Chakraborty and Ray (2006) present a new access control model, called TrustBAC, to address a problem identified in RBAC: difficulty in assigning roles to subjects in decentralized systems, due to the fact that, in this type of systems, identities are often not known a priori and the “user population is dynamic”.

With the proliferation of decentralized systems, developments in the area of access control continue to emerge. Ruj, Nayak, and Stojmenovic (2011) present a new algorithm and model for the access control in clouds by expanding on the cryptographic research previously published. Calero, Edwards, Kirschnick, Wilcock, and Wray (2010) propose a system for the same effect based on the RBAC model. This model intends to describe a suitable architecture for an access control system for cloud computing. Yu, Wang, Ren, and Lou (2010) present their model for access control in cloud computing, which is related to previous research (Calero, Edwards, Kirschnick, Wilcock, & Wray, 2010). Recently, a number of attribute-based access control models have been developed. Ruj, Stojmenovic, and Nayak (2014) present research on access control in decentralized systems in which the identity of the principal is unknown. The research presented (Ruj, Stojmenovic, & Nayak, 2014) extends what had already been done by Ruj, Stojmenovic, and Nayak (2012).

Blockchain

Blockchain is an emerging technology that stems from the combination of previously known research into a cohesive technology that can be used to empowered decentralized applications. Starting in 2008 (Nakamoto, 2008), the research over blockchain has been rising and multiple applications have been created and designed to run on top of blockchains. In this section, the state of the art over blockchain is reviewed.

Background

Chaum (1985) presents research, covering a new approach to digital transactions that took advantage of digital signatures to improve the anonymity of subjects in said transactions. This research presented three use-case from consumer transactions that could potentially benefit from this approach: communications, payments, and credentials. The research presented intended to create a system that allowed for secure, trusted, digital transactions which were untraceable and private.

Nakamoto (2008) developed the first implementation and proposal of what would be Bitcoin which was a completely decentralized digital currency. This proposal for Bitcoin was implemented by recording hashes for digital transactions in an “ongoing chain of hash-based proof-of-work”. Effectively, this solution for the double-spending problem, using a blockchain in a public ledger, was what is now called as a blockchain, although the concept had previously been introduced by Haber and Stornetta (1990). The technology behind blockchain, as developed by Nakamoto (2008), involved previous academic research matched together, in previously unknown ways. Previous attempts at digital currencies had been proposed but none reached the popularity or implementation effectiveness of Bitcoin.

Previous research from Ralph C. Merkle was extensively used to finally advance technology to the point where a Bitcoin implementation is possible. Merkle’s research over public key cryptosystems (Merkle, 1980), was the source for the usage of what is known as Merkle trees. Haber and Stornetta (1990), Haber and Stornetta (1997), and Bayer, Haber, and Stornetta (1993) developed research over the subject of digital time-stamping documents.

Nakamoto (2008) coined the notion of a public transaction ledger that is decentralized by nature. Further research on this topic (Buterin, 2013) created the Ethereum project, which was further discussed byWood (2014). More recently, Garay, Kiayias, and Leonardos (2015) presented a deep analysis over the research that was proposed in Nakamoto (2008), and what the “Bitcoin protocol” formally is made of and suggest as future research the possibility of other kinds of applications being built on top of this protocol and public ledger. Eyal, Gencer, Sirer, and Van Renesse (2016) propose a new blockchain protocol to improve over what has been done previously in Nakamoto (2008).

Applications and Implementations

Dorri, Kanhere, and Jurdak (2016) propose the use of blockchain to improve security over IoT devices. Fotiou and Polyzos (2016) demonstrate how it is possible to use blockchains as the backbone of a decentralized security systems for content distribution. Xu et al. (2016) explore the rationale behind using blockchain as a backbone for large, decentralized and transactional data-sharing environments of untrusted participants, its trade-offs and qualities. Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, and Ait Ouahman (2017) present a state of the art review about access control in IoT devices, in which future research is about the possible use of blockchain as an access control infrastructure in IoT.

More recently, Augot, Chabanne, and George (2017) present a way to perform identity management on the Bitcoin blockchain. Maesa, Ricci, and Mori (2017) present a distributed access control system that functions on top of the a blockchain, based on previous research (Maesa, Mori, & Ricci, 2017). Pilkington, 2015 also presents an analysis over the concepts involving blockchain as well as some of the possible applications, including Access Control applications.

ENTERPRISE ACCESS CONTROL CHALLENGES AND RISKS

The previous section of this chapter was focused on performing a literature review on the extant literature regarding access control, but also new technological paradigms and research that will be further discussed in the following sections. In this section, the authors will review the current challenges and risks existing in the field of access control, particularly in regards to decentralized environments. An analysis of technological challenges and risks will be performed, exposing examples and use-cases in each described challenge or risk. This section intends to expose how, in the current technological landscape, a lack of control over access to data, as well as a lack of cyber security experts over this matter is contributing to an increase in global digital risks.

Technological challenges and risks are inherent to any digital environment. No solution is perfect and there will always be challenges to be overcome and risks to mitigate. Nonetheless, it is important that, when developing access control systems and policies or designing enforcement mechanisms, an analysis of current challenges and risk be performed. A detailed analysis will allow for a deeper understanding of how the solutions proposed and future research directions are a fit for the current challenges and risk. Each of these challenges bears its own relevance but, and more importantly, together they are a recipe for increased risks for businesses. Although not all of these can be directly attributed to a cyber security shortage, that shortage is directly contributing to a decreased capacity to react to these events.

In an increasingly digital world, businesses are intertwined and are directly affected with the technological challenges and risks, but the impact, perception, and outcome are rarely understood a priori. There is a symbiotic relationship between technology and businesses in the sense that the actions of one have impact on the other. The challenges and risks faced in the technological landscape have a direct impact on businesses due to the fact that businesses rely on technology for their day-to-day operations. However, at the same time, some of the risks and challenges that businesses face today are one of the reasons for the technological challenges in the sense that business’ motivations are one of the driving factors of technological innovation.

Emerging Technologies

The technological landscape has been in a constant state of disruption for the past two decades via Artificial Intelligence, Internet of Things, Self-Driving Vehicles, Cryptocurrencies and Blockchain, Social Networks, Smartphones, Cloud Computing and Services, Augmented Reality, Speech Recognition or Virtual Reality. These are all emerging technologies or fields that will be present, in one form or another, in the following digital decades. Each of the listed technologies bears with it increasing security risks and challenges, and paradigm-shifting approaches. Having said that, we can expect that with a global shortage of cyber security professionals, the risks and challenges brought forth by these emerging technologies will have increasing negative outcomes.

This is currently one of the biggest challenges for access control. The number of emerging technologies, and the pace at which new technologies are emerging will pose challenges and risks for access control. These challenges and risks will appear at different layers of the access control paradigms: policy design, management and enforcement, as well as specific implementations, designed and implemented with each of these technologies in mind. Similar to what has been described in previous research (e.g., Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, & Ait Ouahman, 2017), a modern approach to access control should be concerned with providing ”many and diverse approaches” (p. 242) rather than a ”one-size-fits-all approach” (p. 242). Only in this manner will access control be able to adapt to an ever increasing number of emerging technologies and paradigms.

The Internet of Things is currently one of the most interesting examples of this. Recently, highly complex botnets – such as the Mirai botnet – have been used to increase the power and volume of cyber attacks by connecting millions of IoT devices, which are largely unsecure and managed by users that lack the cyber security knowledge to protect themselves from these attacks. How to protect IoT devices is one of the most interesting questions currently in Access Control due to the fact that IoT devices are complexity distributed, devices are mostly independent from each other, and there is difficulty in protecting each device without restricting their users from accessing the functionality in remote manners.

Similarly, self-driving vehicles are another complex device to protect. All in all, a self driving vehicle is very similar to an IoT device, in the sense that it can be seen as a distributed node, which is not meant to be managed by its users, in terms of security, and thus is exposed to similar attack vectors, and shares the same challenges in protection as IoT devices. Access Control research needs to adapt and evolve in order to be able to protect, effectively, and integrate with these new technologies. This is one of the biggest challenges that Access Control faces at the present time.

Lack of Standardization

Similar to what has been described in the section above, Access Control research will also need to be able to embrace and define new standards, in order to effective. This is not a contradiction with the research previously cited via Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, and Ait Ouahman (2017), but rather one of the approaches that need to be taken to effectively be able to tackle the increasing number of emerging technologies.

The argument for this is that with so many emerging technologies, there is an increasing need to embrace standardization in order not to have conflicting solutions for the same issues and, at the same time, in order to have standard ways of proceeding for each specific case. Each of the previous referenced types of access control (DAC, MAC, RBAC and ABAC) were created in an effort to standardize the approach taken to solve some of the problems in control of access, in different contexts.

Recently, there has been an effort in consolidating the existing knowledge for the Attribute-based Access Control and provide a unified definition (Hu et al., 2014). Nonetheless, there’s still a need for global embracement of the standards, as the industry as not yet caught up with these models.

Inflexibility of Policy Management and Ineffective Policy Enforcement

Bauer, Cranor, Reeder, Reiter, and Vaniea (2009) have found in a report over existing real-life challenges in management of access control that some of the larger issues referenced by stakeholders is that access control software is inflexible. Current access control systems are not designed for the existing landscape and, therefore, result in decrease workforce productivity when used completely, incorrect policy design and implementation or in decreased correct usage of the systems. As was analyzed by Bauer, Cranor, Reeder, Reiter, and Vaniea (2009), current tools fail to provide sufficient resources for policy management (p. 899), specifically:

  • • Tools have trouble acknowledging that policy is mostly management by several different members of the workforce. Not by one single entity.
  • • Tools ignore the fact that there exist several layers of policy and, consequently, different policy professionals with different roles and responsibilities.
  • • Not all policy definitions can be enforced completely by existing tools which leads to policy not being implemented, or being incorrectly implemented.

This inflexibility of the policy management tools is an increasing risk to the technological landscape because it supports incorrect usage of policy management tools and enforces incorrect implementations of those policies.

Unsuitability of Existing Access Control Models

As was discussed in the literature review, one of the current trends in access control research is over the applicability of current defined access control models over these new paradigms. This is a challenge because current access control models took decades to develop and are increasingly ineffective for the current technological landscape.

Dynamic Threats

Potential threats to technological systems are increasingly more dynamic and relying on different aspects of the environment, mostly due to the fact that the technological systems have themselves become increasingly more distributed and dynamic. Current threats are no longer static and they evolve and modify themselves along with their environment. This poses new and challenging risks to access control because access control can no longer rely on a static set of objects and subject.

Landscape Complexity, Decentralization and Innovation

Along with the emergence of new technologies, we are also witnessing an increasing complexity, decentralization and innovation in the technological landscape. New approaches are becoming standards and old standards are becoming irrelevant. Infrastructure is becoming more and more relevant, with the rise of DevOps, Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery. Landscapes are becoming increasingly distributed and, in some cases, increasingly decentralized, which poses new challenges to the way access control is practiced.

Lack of Collaborative Tools

Along with the inflexibility of policy management tools, there is also a lack of collaborative tools that correctly and safely integrate with the access control level desired by most applications. This leads to corruption of the access control flows, such as downloading files and sharing them with fellow co-workers, that generate new risks for businesses. This lack of collaborative tools and access control systems that are capable of handling collaboration effectively is inherently a technological challenge that is exposed by the lack of reaction to the digital landscape and workforce changes, which require more collaboration in increasingly digital form.

Increasing Attack Vectors and Attack Volume

We have seen an increase in attack vectors and volume of attacks over the past years. This is only expected to worsen in the coming years due to the shortage of effective access control systems and shortage of cybersecurity professionals to design and enforce policies, and systems, correctly.

SOLUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The authors have described in the Background section on a high-level the existing literature over the applications of blockchain-based technologies to the challenges of access control. In this section, we will analyze that literature at a deeper level to argue how blockchain-based technologies can be one of the leading solutions for mitigating the current access control challenges that the technological landscape presents as described in the previous section. This section also proposes a high-level approach that can enable businesses to take advantage of blockchain-based technologies to enhance the security of their access control mechanisms.

Reasons for Blockchain

The concept of a blockchain fits perfectly with the properties that we desire in access control: traceability, scalability, reliability, immutability and decentralization. This is shown to be true by reviewing research for Bitcoin (Nakamoto, 2008), sequential research over Ethereum (Buterin, 2013; Wood, 2014) and numerous existing blockchain-based applications (Pilkington, 2016; Augot et al., 2017). We will proceed to describe below how blockchain complements each of these characteristics.

A guarantee of immutability emerges from the concept of the blockchain, which is a chain of blocks with each block having a connection to the previous one, thus making tampering the existing data extremely difficult (Nakamoto, 2008; Haber & Stornetta, 1991, 1997; Bayer et al., 1993; Eyal et al., 2016). Improved traceability is a consequence of immutability. Relying on the chain of blocks, each transaction (Nakamoto, 2008; David Chaum, 1985; D. Chaum, 1988; Merkle, 1980) is recorded inside the blockchain and it cannot be changed. This allows for the inspection of the blockchain and each of its transactions, guaranteeing traceability capacities for the environment.

Due to the fact that we are creating a peer-to-peer decentralized network of nodes that are all connected and communicating, the scalability of the network, using blockchain, is enhanced (Nakamoto, 2008; Castro and Liskov, 1999). New nodes can be added more easily than with a centralized solution, as well, the network can grow and adapt to the number of subjects using it. Since each node has its own copy of the database and can act as an authority for itself, the use of blockchain guarantees there is no single point of failure, like a centralized solution would have, thus enhancing the reliability of access control and, consequently, further decentralization of access control (Nakamoto, 2008; Wood, 2014).

The statements above intend to demonstrate how blockchain’s inherent characteristics are a perfect match for the characteristics we desire to obtain, on our approach, and to use as a means to enhance access control capabilities.

Applications of Blockchain in Existing Literature

Starting with the Internet of Things research, Dorri, Kanhere, and Jurdak (2016) propose in a position paper a “new secure, private and lightweight architecture for IoT” (p. 1), based on blockchain technology to protect IoT devices. In this research, a theoretical architecture is proposed under a smart homes’ case study that interacts with the blockchain to ensure privacy and enhanced security. The architecture presented in this research utilizes overlay networks, similar to peer-to-peer networks, connected over the Tor protocol, to conceal sensitive data from potential attacks.

This research has been evaluated qualitatively only against a set of common attack vectors to analyze the potential for real-life usage. Although it faces challenges argued in the paper, such vulnerabilities to denial of service attacks or 51% attacks, in which an attacker holds more than 50% of the entire network, it can be considered as a starting point for blockchain-based access control in IoT devices and networks. In this sense, there remains a need for implementation results to further validate this type of research. What Dorri, Kanhere, and Jurdak (2016) propose is further validated by an extensive state of the art report conducted by Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, and Ait Ouahman (2017), in which the following is stated:

The development of autonomous, decentralized architectures and the location of intelligence mainly security and access control logics at the very edge of the networks are issues that need to be addressed. (p. 257)

This research further validates the proposal that a decentralized architecture for access control, in which security logic is embedded at the edge of the networks, might not only be possible but desirable. Moving away from IoT, research over security for content distribution has been proposed by Fotiou and Polyzos (2016) using blockchains. By leveraging blockchain-based technology, Fotiou and Polyzos (2016) are able to disseminate parameters of the content owner to the network in a decentralized architecture.

This research represents an evolution in Information Content Networks’ control of access, that overcomes challenges in data dissemination by using blockchain-based technologies. This research also overcomes one of the issues with the previous described research because a prototype implementation was developed that helps validate this approach, and validate the data distribution power of blockchain-based technologies.

Interesting research also exists on the topic of using blockchain-based technologies as a “software connector” (Xu et al., 2016, p. 182):

We found that using the blockchain as a software connector could improve information transparency and traceability.

Although this research does not necessarily mention access control, it is relevant to our use case because it argues that blockchain-based technologies can, in fact, be used as an enhancement mechanism, inside a software architecture, to enhance properties of “security, privacy, scalability and sustainability” (p. 182). An interesting fact about this research is that, although it has serves only as a position paper, it has roots and knowledge that have been gathered from implementation projects using blockchain-based technologies. This fact reinforces the authors confidence in the applicability of blockchain-based technologies in real-life challenges, specifically in access control challenges. Additionally, it is worth mentioning this research starts mentioning the important concept of a private blockchain, which will be further discussed below.

Similarity, and while we are discussing the concept of a private blockchain, this concept has been research extensively by Pilkington (2016) which offers the following definition:

In a fully private ledger, write-permissions are monitored by a central locus of decision-making. Read-permissions are either public or restricted (Buterin, 2015b). A private blockchain amounts to a permissioned ledger, whereby an organizational process of Know-Your-Business (KYB) and Know-Your-Customer (KYC) enables the white listing (or blacklisting) of user identity. (p. 236)

The concept of private blockchains is very relevant in an enterprise ecosystem because truly public blockchains cannot provide the guarantees that enterprise environments need in terms of the nodes that have write and read access to the blockchain. Controlling who has write and read permissions to the blockchain does not necessarily invalidate the concept of a blockchain, but rather it reduces costs and improves the applicability of blockchain-based solutions in private environments, as a way to decentralize solutions, as is also pointed in the same research:

The public vs private blockchain debate comes down to a bifurcation between permisionned and permissionless validators (Swanson, 2015, p.25). Yet, “the bifurcationists are not saying one approach is better than the other, rather, they each solve different problems” (ibid.). The blockchain world is an abstract space between the public ledger database and the purely private blockchain: “the defining characteristic of this space is the idea of decentralization. But don't think decentralization versus centralization. Think in terms of a continuum” (Brown, 2014). (p. 245)

Pilkington (2016) laid, in a very structural way, the defining concepts of different ways of using the blockchains. Furthermore, this research has also produced some use cases for the application of blockchain-based technologies, such as digital identity providers, voting systems, finance industry services, supply-chain enhancements and, of course, cryptocurrencies.

Another application of blockchain-based technologies found in existing literature is that of Identity Management. Augot, Chabanne, and George (2017) have proposed that blockchain-based technologies be used as validators against digital assured identities. This research is relevant in the sense that it starts using blockchain-based technologies not only as the backbone of decentralized software architectures, but also as a means to improve current day-to-day business operations by providing a way for users to have digital anonymous identities that can be validated against, without any previous knowledge on the part of the validators over the users’ real identity.

Finally, there’s already initial research over the application of blockchain-based technologies for access control. Maesa, Ricci, and Mori (2017) have proposed research based on deeper research by Maesa, Mori, and Ricci (2017) that effectively applies blockchain-based technologies, in this case the public Bitcoin blockchain, to store access control policies. This proposal is an entire new approach that is a starting point towards what has been argued in this chapter: the application of blockchain-based technologies to access control systems to offer an alternative solution that can effectively tackle the challenges which the current technological landscape poses. The solution proposed in this research uses the Bitcoin blockchain to store the rights of a subject to access a resource with improve traceability and auditability properties. This research offers a prototype implementation using the Bitcoin blockchain that validates the approach suggested but, at the same time, difficultes the usage of it, from an enterprise perspective due to high costs, high transaction times and reduced privacy inherent to the Bitcoin blockchain.

The previous paragraphs serve, in the context of this chapter, to demonstrate and validate that blockchain-based technologies can, in fact, be considered as a solution for several of the problems of access control that we have described in previous sections.

Using Permissioned Blockchains

Throughout the previous the authors have described existing literature that supports a solution to current access control challenges on top of blockchain-based technologies, as well as reasons for why blockchain-based technologies fit in within the access control subject, at all. One key concept of this proposal, and one that is worth retaining, is that the approach suggested in this chapter is based mostly on the use of private decentralized ledgers. Private blockchains set themselves apart from public blockchains by having access control in place for the actual ledger, for reading from and writing to the ledger (Pilkington, 2016). Thus, private blockchains are more suitable for enterprise-level decentralized access control because they offer most of the benefits of blockchains with less security and privacy risks.

Modern open-source platforms such as Hyperledger Sawtooth or Hyperledger Fabric ease the development and implementation of private blockchains by providing tools that established the foundations of such projects. With such projects it is possible to instantiate a blockchain within an organization’s private network, controlling access to it through built-in access control mechanisms, thus creating a private blockchain. These sorts of projects introduce modulars platform for a modern implementation of applications on top of permissioned distributed ledgers. They can be used as the backbone of specific implementations.

As explained earlier, permissioned decentralized ledger are more suitable for enterprise-level access control, but it must still be customized to be suitable for specific purposes. Instead of using a public blockchain which goes against what most enterprises desire, private blockchains can be built using Hyperledger Sawtooth or Hyperledger Fabric. These platforms offers a complete set of tools to build applications on top of a distributed ledger that include: REST APIs, a validator network, permissioned capabilities, events, custom transaction processors, a consensus protocol, defined as Proof of Elapsed Time, that is less computationally expensive, and, of course, a distributed ledger with all its core functionality. To connect all the pieces together it offers Software Development Kits, in a variety of languages such as Java, Python, Go or Javascript, easing the development prototypes. In the case of Hyperledger Fabric, its offers a wide array of different features, such as a smart contracts’ engine which, dependending on specific needs might more suitable than simply writing/reading from the distributed ledger. These tools increase the usability and applicability of permissioned distributed ledgers in access control, in enterprise ecosystems.

Another relevant framework, which can be used with blockchain-based technologies and has been used in previous research (Maesa, Ricci, & Mori, 2017; Maesa, Mori, & Ricci, 2017), is the eXtensible Access Control Markup Language (Oasis, 2013), specifically Version 3.0 of the standard. XACML 3.0 is an OASIS language whose purpose is to standardize the way in which access control policies are written. Much like SAML for authentication, XACML offers a wide array of standards that can be used as guidelines. Using XACML allows to write prototypes that are according to best practices in enterprise-level information security and access control. The use of XACML is quite justified when reading the beginning of the standard:

(..), there is a pressing need for a common language for expressing security policy. If implemented throughout an enterprise, a common policy language allows the enterprise to manage the enforcement of all the elements of its security policy in all the components of its information systems.

By using XACML and permissioned blockchains, enterprise solutions can be designed for access control by leveraging private blockchain-based technologies as a way to store and distribute authorizations within decentralized environments. Decentralized ledgers, in this approach, are used as a technological component that is the backbone for access control, with which the challenges exposed earlier can be faced and mitigated. Using a permissioned decentralized ledger, as the basis of solutions, it is possible to aim at the decentralization of:

  • • Policy Enforcement Point.
  • • Policy Decision Point.
  • • Policy Administration Point.
  • • Policy Information Point.

Facing the Challenges

In previous sections we have described existing literature that supports the usage of blockchain-based technologies in access control to mitigate the challenges it faces. Furthermore, we have also argued how solutions based on permissioned blockchains might be a relevant topic for research in face of this challenges. In this section we will briefly describe how the challenges and risks, described before, are directly affected with what has been proposed in this chapter.

The approach suggested in this chapter relies on a paradigm-shifting mentality that is starting to emerge across the access control community. As we have shown previously, increasingly more research has been developed with the focus on providing concrete access control solutions to specific problems in a diverse technological landscape. By using permissioned ledgers, we can leverage the inherent properties of blockchains to faced the emerging technologies, at a global scale.

Blockchains are technology agnostic and can be the backbone of solutions that improve the way access control policy and authorization distribution occurs for different sets of ever expanding technologies. By using blockchains, access control solutions also become more dynamic in the way they distribute data, and decentralized, allowing for a more rapid reaction to ever more dynamic threats, hopefully reducing both the attack vectors available and the volume of attacks, by improving the security of enterprises and devices, and mitigating single points of failure.

At the same time, blockchains also offer the possibility of spreading access control to the edges of increasingly complex and decentralized networks, in an effective manner. By using XACML, and similar standards, as well as Attribute-based Access Control models, this approach intends to guide access control systems, and practitioners, to embrace standardization, improving the overall security of systems, as well as well as forcing the design of access control mechanisms that are a better fit for the existing technological landscape. Offering more dynamic access control policies also impacts the flexibility of policy management and improves the effectiveness of policy enforcement - improving the way in which workforce can collaborate.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

The field of Access Control has a mission to always be producing knowledge that is able to control access to data in all the diverse manners that the industry presents to it. Therefore, the authors consider that some interesting discussions are still relevant, at this moment, such as:

  • • Public vs Permissioned Blockchains: As mentioned previously, both approaches have their pros and cons but, in essence, the applicability of each of the approaches lies on the context, objectives and desired outcome. It is important that discussions over the best approach, for different parameters emerge, in the future, in order to grant it a more relevant research niche and to be able to research past that foundational concept.
  • • Diversified Approaches: More and diversified approaches are needed for decentralization of access control are needed, fitting the specifics of each use-case that exists. The reason for this is, as was argued before and is present in previous research (Ouaddah, Mousannif, Abou Elkalam, & Ait Ouahman, 2017), that access control will tend to focus less on generic approaches and more on use-case focused approaches. That being said, a diverse set of solid approach is relevant to improve the current state of decentralized access control.
  • • Moving Past Theoretical Research: In order for this type of research to be successful, there is a need for researchers to move past theoretical research into more applicable research. We have mentioned a series of research that propose new approaches and architectures but there’s a need for effective research that can be applied in enterprise ecosystems.

There is an emerging trend over the applicability of applications built on top of blockchain-based solutions, which has seen increased research over the years since the concept was first presented, in 2008, for the Bitcoin cryptocurrency (Nakamoto, 2008). Apart from access control, the concept of blockchains will have a tremendous business impact in several industries, be it supply-chain management, financial services or healthcare. It has the potential of revolutionizing the way untrusted entities and devices interact with each other. For these reasons, it becomes even more relevant for access control to be able to offer solutions that can integrate with blockchain.

Furthermore, due to the increasingly decentralized technological landscape we are witnessing, it makes sense for access control to be capable of offering a solution that is inherently decentralize but still secure. The authors believe that this emerging intersection between Access Control and Blockchain is a research field that offers immense potential and research opportunities, due to the amount of innovation witnessed and the challenges we still face today.

CONCLUSION

Access Control is still an exciting field, full of innovation and challenges. Throughout this chapter, an extensive review of the literature was conducted in Access Control, as well as a brief overview of Blockchain research. The review of literature had two objectives: understand the challenges and gaps that access control still presents today, as well as start to analyze emerging technologies that can be a starting point for enhanced access control, specifically, blockchain-based technologies.

We have further analyzed a collection of challenges in enterprise access control that originate from the conducted review of literature. These include emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things, or cloud services; lack of standardization, in implementations across the industry; inflexibility of policy management, that stems from the inflexibility of the existing solutions, which originates ineffective policy enforcement, increasing risk or constraining user actions; unsuitability of existing access control models, to face the challenges presented by the industry; a growing number of attack vectors and more dynamic threats; increasing complexity, decentralization and innovation in the existing technological landscape; and a lack of solutions that allow for effective collaboration, internally, within organizations. These challenges and risks call for a review of the paradigm and approaches to access control.

With this in mind, this chapter proposes blockchain-based solutions as a new approach to access control implementation, further decentralizing access control and improving key properties of it. The authors have argued how blockchains’ inherent properties allow for a more dynamic approach to access control that can help mitigate the technological challenges present previously.

Underwood, S. (2016). Blockchain Beyond Bitcoin. Communications of the ACM , 59(11), 15–17. doi:10.1145/2994581

Yermack, D. (2017). Corporate Governance and Blockchains. Review of Finance , 21(1), 7–31. doi:doi:10.1093/rof/rfw074

Zyskind, G., Nathan, O., & Pentland, A. ’. (2015). Decentralizing Privacy: Using Blockchain to Protect Personal Data. In 2015 IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW) (pp. 180–184). IEEE. doi:10.1109/SPW.2015.27

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Access Control: The approval or rejection of access from a specific subject to a specific resource.

Access Control Model: Conceptual model by which access control is designed, managed, and enforced in a specific context.

Blockchain: Decentralized ledger, whose data and integrity are maintained and validated by a collection of participants in a network through consensus protocols.

Decentralized Network: A distributed network that lacks a central authority and maintains consensus between the participants in the network through consensus protocols.

Distributed Network: A network whose participants and stakeholders are distributed either geographically or virtually. A distributed network can be decentralized whenever it lacks a central point of authority; in other cases, it remains a centralized distributed network.

Internet of Things: Network of physical devices embedded with electronic components that allow them to connect with each other and exchange information.

Permissioned Blockchain: A blockchain in which control of read and/or write permissions can be managed for the entire network or a subset of its nodes.

Private Blockchain: A blockchain that is not accessible to the general public and is not therefore readable or writable by the public. These blockchains can be permissioned or lack permissioned capabilities. Examples of private blockchains are blockchains hidden behind firewall or internal to a specific organization.

Public Blockchain: Blockchains that are accessible either to read and/or write publicly to any interested party.
