KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Computer Network: A set of computers connected together for the purpose of sharing resources.

Cybercriminal: An individual who commits computer-related crimes.

Cybersecurity: The protection of systems, networks, and data in cyberspace.

Cyberspace: Cyberspace is a domain characterized by the use of electronics and the electromagnetic spectrum to store, modify, and exchange data via networked systems and associated physical infrastructures.

Data Security: The practice of keeping data protected from corruption and unauthorized access.

Digital Society: A modern society is a progressive society that is formed as a result of the adoption and integration of information and communication technologies.

Encryption: The process of converting information or data into a code to prevent unauthorized access.

Ransom: Money paid or demanded for the release of someone or something from captivity.

Security Patch: A fix to program that eliminates a vulnerability exploited by malicious hackers.

Vulnerability: The quality of being easily hurt or attacked.

Chapter 11

Mass-Scale Human Cognitive Limits to Explain the “Weakest Link” in Cybersecurity

  • Shalin Hai-Jew
    Kansas State University, USA

ABSTRACT

If people are the “weakest link” in cybersecurity because of their psychological make-up and hardwiring—their socialized desire to trust and cooperate with others, their cognitive biases and misperceptions, their preferences for convenience, their general going with System 1 inattention instead of System 2 attention and thinking—this begs the question of whether the same micro-scale cognitive limits found in individual users are also present on a mass scale. After all, there have been discovered problematic unthinking leanings in group decision making: obedience to authority, bystander effects, groupthink, and the Abilene paradox, among others. Using a range of often mass-scale data sources and data analytics tools, research questions were asked around three areas: (1) the level of sophistication of the cybersecurity electronic hive mind towards cybersecurity issues, (2) the gap between the non-expert members and the expert members in the hive mind, and (3) whether the extant hive mind was more reflective of mob unthinkingness or deliberation and wisdom.

INTRODUCTION

In every chain of reasoning, the evidence of the last conclusion can be no greater than that of the weakest link of the chain, whatever may be the strength of the rest. – Thomas Reid in Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man – (1786)

A chain is only as strong as its weakest link. – a common saying

Intelligence is highly improbable, and collective intelligence is even more so. It runs into misinformation, misjudgment, and misunderstanding. This is unavoidable because thinking is a site for conflict, tactics, and strategies. Insight jumps out of the clash of argument as well as linear discovery of truths. – Geoff Mulgan (2018), in Big Mind: How Collective Intelligence Can Change Our World (p. 126)

Online is where a large portion of the world’s population live and breathe and have their being. As the cyber footprint is broadened—through mobile devices, locational apps, games, smart cars, medical devices, and the Internet of Things (IoT)—there are that many more potential attack surfaces through which people may be affected negatively through hacks and cyberattacks. Adam Segal (2016) writes: “An estimated 75 percent of the world’s population now has access to a mobile phone, and the Internet connects 40 percent of the planet’s population, roughly 2.7 billion people. Information and communications networks are embedded in our political, economic, and social lives.” (p. 1). He predicts an intensification of the battle over cyberspace, with Year Zero of this battle starting June, 2012 or June, 2013, given a number of high profile uses of cyberattacks by nation states. In 2016, there were four billion cyberattacks, a major jump from the 600 million in 2015 (IBM, as cited in Balaish, Aug. 21, 2017). By 2021, cyber crime is estimated to cost US$2 trillion (Cybersecurity Ventures, as cited in Balaish, 2017). Cybersecurity efforts focus on preventing the illegal exploitation of technology systems and the protection of data integrity, among other things.

In cybersecurity studies and practices, humans are known as “the weakest link” (Belbey, 2015); their decisions and actions put their information at risk and also those of others. Humans will use and re-use weak passwords or leave passwords unchanged from factory defaults; they over-share with friends, family, and strangers; they click unthinkingly on risky links and download files (with malware) from others; they will receive emails from strangers or apparent colleagues and click on links or download files without thinking; they’ll receive USB drives at conferences and use these in their laptops and desktops; they’ll download apps from unknown websites; they will visit the Web’s dark spaces to buy illicit goods; they’re prone to being social engineered; and they do not begin to understand the “cyber” threats arrayed against them.

One way to begin to understand why people are so vulnerable to cyber-exploitation is to not only explore people and their individual cognitive limits and biases but also to explore the “electronic hive mind” around cybersecurity to understand mass-scale human cognitive limits and biases. A “mind” refers to consciousness, thinking, intellect, and will. A “hive mind” refers “group intelligence” (Jones, 2011, p. 2). A hive mind refers to the consciousness, thinking, intellect, and will of a collective of people. Such collectives occur organically, with people coming together around shared interests. A core purpose of a hive mind is to learn from the environment, from others outside the hive, and from each other. Bloom’s taxonomy of learning domains types (1956) can apply to group intelligence: the steps include remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, and creating. (Conceptualize teams collaborating around shared research and design and development work.) As in learning communities, consensus and dissensus are both important. Certainly, if hive minds can function like individual ones, they can also be misled, misinformed, irrational, and deluded.

A hive mind does not have centralized control; rather, control is distributed and devolved, with each member and small groups within the collective making decisions, sharing ideas, and taking actions. How these hive minds coalesce and evolve is determined in part by the group impetuses and interests, and evolved social norms. Hive minds can be informed by co-created culture. In the same that that the cultural features of a society may head off some possible futures and make others more likely (Dieffenbach, 1992), how “hive” populations evolve may also change.

From localized and small acts of individual members, it is possible for emergent patterns of intelligence and self-organizing behavior to emerge at the macro level. The purpose of a hive mind is conceptualized as promotion of the hive’s (population’s) survival. A hive mind has been referred to as “swarm intelligence” and “collective consciousness.” The macro consciousness can create new insights and can act as a macro-entity en masse towards shared aims (such as advocating particular government policies, for example).

In such contexts, in which information is shared openly and broadly, individual expertise no longer holds the command it once did. One researcher explains:

If we can easily exchange large chunks of knowledge and are connected by high-bandwidth communication paths, the function and purpose served by individuals becomes unclear. Individuals have served to keep the gene pool stirred up and healthy via sexual reproduction, but this data handling process would no longer necessarily be linked to individuals. With knowledge no longer encapsulated in individuals, the distinction between individuals and the entirety of humanity would blur. Think Vulcan mind-meld. We would perhaps become more of a hive mind — an enormous, single, intelligent entity. (Burger, 2002, p. 150)

And yet, the contributions of experts to a hive mind are critical for understandings and guidance. Without expertise, it is difficult to place current events into context. It is difficult to vet complex information. The germane cognitive load of cybersecurity is demanding, and expertise itself is difficult to find. One author has pointed to the pendulum in the U.S. swinging too far to the side of non-expertise and even self-ignorance. He writes:

In the end, expertise is difficult to define, and experts are sometimes hard to tell from dilettantes. Still, we should be able to distinguish between people who have a passing acquaintance with a subject and people whose knowledge is definitive. No one’s knowledge is complete, and experts realize this better than anyone. But education, training, practice, experience, and acknowledgment by others in the same field should provide us with at least a rough guide to dividing experts from the rest of society. (Nichols, 2017, p. 39)

Worse yet, experts may have high WTGA tendencies (“willing to give advice”) even outside of their areas of expertise or with carelessness which renders their suggestions not particularly valuable (Dillon & Carlson, 2017). While online communities are open spaces with people coming and going as they choose, the relevance of expertise might suggest that newbies should be constantly striving towards expertise and not fronting knowledge or skills that they do not possess. One example of hive mind collaboration is from “folk” or non-expert tagging of contents on the Web.

Today, users are adding metadata and using tags to organize their own digital collections, categorize the content of others and build bottom-up classification systems. The wisdom of crowds, the hive mind, and the collective intelligence are doing what heretofore only expert catalogers, information architects and website authors have done. They are categorizing and organizing the Internet and determining the user experience, and it’s (sic) working. No longer do the experts have the monopoly on this domain; in this new age users have been empowered to determine their own cataloging needs. Metadata is now in the realm of the Everyman. (Kroski, 2005, p. 1)

Another example in the research literature refers to the hive mind’s usage in enhancing collaborative design (Zhu, Mussio, & Barricelli, 2010).

Hive minds are not purposively created per se, but they emerge based on how individual actors make choices and how they behave. (This “emergent” phenomenon is observed in a variety of natural contexts. It is often modeled using agent-based modeling…to show how simple rules based on simple choices of the respective agents can form over-arching patterns.)

Each member of the community interacts locally with a limited set of other members of the community and with the environment according to local rules of behavior and communication. Each member follows the local rules of interaction and communication according to her/his experience, skill and knowledge. Even in absence of any centralized control, a global behavior emerges from local interactions, which is unknown to individual members of the community and not predictable by external observers. In the virtual world, online communities harness the Web technology to build collective intelligence which only experts, information architects and website developers could achieve before…In all these domains, communities of users find a virtual place were to congregate and collaborate, supporting one another, creating and sharing their own data and metadata on the Internet. (Zhu, Mussio, & Barricelli, 2010, p. 124)

Even without a centralized executive control, hive minds enable people to cooperate, collaborate, and co-create; it enables them to take part in shared endeavors larger than the individual. The “hive mind” is conceptualized as “a collective attribute of humanity” that makes possible large-scale endeavors, based on information, intercommunications, and “simultaneous action” (Dalley, 2014, pp. 82 – 83). The hive mind is enhanced and empowered by technologies:

All of these characteristics of the Hive Mind are demonstrable without technology. However, when they are supported by technology their effects increase exponentially. It is technology that is revealing our Hive Mind characteristics. The printing press, the telescope, the computer, the Internet, and mobile devices all give us visibility into how our Hive Mind operates. The technology gives us visibility into Hive Mind operations via psychological projections. (Dalley, 2014, pp. 82 – 83)

These technologies enable collaboration across global-scale distances and time. In a culture of participation, they enable the existence of “electronic hive minds,” the distributed consciousness of people with shared interests. As entities, electronic hive minds are built on the substructures of the Internet (aka the “Fifth Estate”), the World Wide Web (particularly Web 2.0 or the Social Web), social media platforms, and communications technologies. Socio-technical spaces have been created to enable people to collaborate, to share endeavors, and to keep and maintain personal profiles over time (and even into perpetuity).

The membership in an electronic “hive” is transient, and this is built on interested parties from the world’s electronically connected populations. There are some natural feeder communities in terms of cybersecurity—such as professionals in the field. In terms of non-professionals, there may be hobbyists, amateurs (those who dabble and are fairly well informed but who do not aspire to professional expertise), and novices (those who may aspire to be experts in the field one day). In the electronic hive mind, issues arise and disappear, given the limits of human attention and the speed of information flow.

As with all communities, there are bandwidth limits to attention. The memory behind the hive mind may vary depending on what is archived online and what is taken offline…and also depending on the membership (and the existence of old-timers and mavens). The popularity of a topic may ensure that the topic is top-of-hive-mind for a time but does not ensure long-term focus or interest (or even long-term memory). Participants may share expertise, pose questions (and begin article stubs in crowd-sourced dictionary sites), and engage in other ways.

The capture and archival of electronic desiderata central to the hive mind communicates externalized expressions of the hive mind’s thoughts. The digital contents online created by individuals and groups in the electronic hive mind may extend individual and collective memory for a “shared extended mind”. Not only are these an aide de memoire but enable an exploration of the “electronic hive mind” based on particular shared issues of interest. One authoring team describes this phenomenon this way:

Some types of species exploit the external environment to support their cognitive processes, in the sense of patterns created in the environment that function as external mental states and serve as an extension to their mind. In the case of social species the creation and exploitation of such patterns can be shared, thus obtaining a form of shared mind or collective intelligence. (Bosse, Jonker, Schut, & Treur, 2006, p. 151)

The “hive mind” is more than the sum of its human parts. In a broad sense, the electronic hive mind may be conceptualized as a sentient and potent mass entity with potential for various types of concentrated mass action as well as dispersed smaller-unit actions, among others. From social psychology, analogical “cognitive biases” in group dynamics may be found in research on group decision-making. They include:

  • • a tendency to follow authority figures, with a concomitant unwillingness to challenge them even in ethically challenging situations (“obedience to authority”) (Milgram, 1963);
  • • a tendency to experience a dissipation of individual responsibility and apathy in the presence of a group (“bystander effect” or “diffusion of responsibility (Darley & Latané, 1968);
  • • a tendency towards consensus and “groupthink” (Janis, 1972), and
  • • the occurrence of the “Abilene paradox” based on unthinking acceptance of an initial suggestion (based in part on social conformity) and not considering actual interests (Harvey, 1996)

In work places, healthy group dynamics have to be trained and inculcated. Members are encouraged to share leadership in a distributed way, to be empowered for speaking up and decision-making, to fight “groupthink” (group decision-making without individual responsibility) by having assigned contrarians (based on the 10th man principle) and having diverse members at the table, and to test proposals on a range of metrics to ensure that the decision-making is as optimal as possible. Taleb (2007 / 2010) has suggested that the old model of assessing probabilities with the assumption of an underlying normal frequency distribution is limited and does not prepare people for rare and potentially catastrophic “black swan” and rare and anticipate-able “gray swan” events. The unthinkable has to be thinkable to enable anticipation, psychological readiness, planning, and defense.

Defining a Cybersecurity Electronic Hive Mind

Generally, a hive mind is inclusive of all potential members, no matter what their level of expertise is regarding the target topic. A “cybersecurity” hive mind is comprised of people who interact and engage around this topic, optimally with some regularity. For the interests of this research though, the direct expert expressions and points-of-view are not of direct interest per se. What is more engaging is studying the messages received and understood and engaged and regurgitated by the public non-expert hive mind (in order to compare against expert insights). How does the general public “swarm” the cybersecurity issue, and then how do they reflect or not reflect expert and opinions and insights?

Three general research areas were explored (phrased as related questions):

  • 1. What is the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind in regards to cybersecurity? Are there blind spots (lacunae) regarding cybersecurity? If so, what are these, are they from critical areas of cybersecurity, and why might these exist?
  • 2. How does the folk electronic hive mind differ from the expressions of cybersecurity experts on the Social Web / Web 2.0? If these exist, what are the main differences, and why might these exist?
  • 3. Is the “hive mind” (related to cybersecurity) more reflective of (a) a mob mentality or herd mind, or is it more reflective of (b) collective intelligence and “wisdom of crowds”? Is the hive mind functioning effectively and prosocially regarding cybersecurity (or not)? How so? How not?

Various elements of the mass electronic hive mind relating to cybersecurity were explored to understand mass thinking about cybersecurity. There was information taken from the World Wide Web (WWW), the Internet, and social media platforms, from multimodal digital data sources. The analytical approaches include the following:

  • • Correlated search terms over extended time and at mass scale in Google Search using Google Correlate;
  • • Text analysis of cybersecurity subreddits;
  • • Correlated terms appearing over time in scanned books through the Google Books Ngram Viewer;
  • • #hashtag networks from Twitter;
  • • Social imagery from Google Images and Flickr;
  • • Related tags networks from Flickr;
  • • Audio files in iTunes;
  • • Social videos on YouTube, and
  • • Slideshows on SlideShare.

The focus is on non-expert parts of the hive mind, so contents in academia and the news media were not directly included. Nor were contents from government sources.

The Potential Relevance of Understanding an Electronic Hive Mind Around Cybersecurity

In a cybersecurity context, an electronic hive mind is potentially analytically relevant in several ways: (1) as an indicator of social knowledge regarding cybersecurity, (2) as a problem-solving community, and (3) as a social influence on others.

  • • First, it indicates at a mass scale what the public is thinking about cybersecurity and may be one indicator of how well prepared they are in the face of fairly unrelenting cyberattacks. The messages shared in the hive mind may be generalized out to some degree. It can be informative. The questions being asked by the hive mind, how they go about answering those questions, and what they do with the answers are also relevant. How well the hive mind responds to new information and surprises may be another indicator of health of the hive mind*.
  • • Second, problem-solving may emerge from the electronic hive mind. If parts or the whole of the hive mind decide to take on particular challenges, they can have a powerful influence.
  • • Third, the electronic hive mind also may work as social influence on others. The hive mind can set a standard for “social proof” and in so doing set a standard for larger population readiness, capabilities, and actions. It can play an agenda-setting role in the way that traditional mass media did and how social media do today. In the best case scenarios, the electronic hive mind can serve as early warning of risks and can model proper responses to cyber hazards and threats.

*The first bullet in this section can benefit from elaboration. This hive mind information can be used by cybersecurity experts and communications professionals to target messaging more effectively to strengthen individuals and groups against cybersecurity compromises. This information may inform gaps analyses, with intervention plans built around addressing such gaps. How expert-provided information and media-provided information are echoed back by members of the hive mind may also indicate how well that information has been received and understood and used. Those tasked with cybersecurity policies have a large task building societal capacities by appealing to citizens and their power as voters and taxpayers and users of technologies. There are challenges in terms of attracting public attention and interest, when there may be a low level of interest in the topic. There are challenges with building trust given the public fears of government interference in their lives. There is the difficult message of letting people know that some attitudes, thoughts, and behaviors make people the “weakest link,” but to do so without creating in them a sense of learned helplessness and passivity. It is important to convey the proper sense of threat, again, to change awareness and behavior but without shutting people down.

REVIEW OF THE LITERATURE

When Tim Berners-Lee originated the concept of the World Wide Web and created HyperText Markup Language (HTML), Uniform Resource Identifiers (URI), and Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) (in 1990), and the first web editor/browser and first web server, the initial idea was that the Web would be for people to build web communities (“History of the Web,” 2008 – 2017). Shortly after this spate of creativity, by 1991 people outside of CERN were invited to join the Web. In the intervening years, people started to realize that online security was an issue. There were various endeavors to steal people’s credentials and identities, steal funds, extort individuals, access sensitive intellectual property (IP), lock protected files and demand payment (through ransomware), infringe on privacy, troll and harass individuals, and others. Why there is this state of affairs can be attributed to many reasons.

One common reason that is pointed-to has been the idea that security had not been “baked in” at the beginning. Others have been that software makers have focused a lot of attention on software features, not on security. Nation-states have gotten into the game by setting up units of their respective militaries to exploit the cyber realm. Many also do not enforce cybersecurity regimes among their citizens who exploit other countries’ systems, so such individuals are protected against extradition in these spaces (beyond the reach of Interpol).

There are many cybersecurity responsibilities and efforts that occur outside of mainstream public awareness by governments and corporations. In terms of national security, governments deal with cyber as its own domain and work hard to secure it. There is work in figuring out how best to conceptualize cybersecurity to align the research to best deal with evolving security challenges (Langø, 2013). For governments, there is major interest in protecting critical infrastructure (like power grids); their focus is complex and multi-faceted, focused on “vulnerability, access, and motive” (Koppel, 2015). The private sector has a critical role to play in terms of providing cybersecurity (Etzioni, 2011). The thinking has changed on how to defend technology systems, with multiple defense lines for defense-in-depth (He, Chan, Zhang, Wu, & Wang, 2014, p. 19). For organizations, there are more formalized and structured ways to assess cyber vulnerabilities and enhancing preparedness (Johnson 2004).

There are studies on how people respond in disasters and some of their actions or non-actions may compound the risk. In mass-scale challenges, there is the need to make “new instincts” (Ripley, 2008, p. 203) and to build capacity and resilience.

Dealing With Cybersecurity Threats

The general public may choose to engage with cybersecurity threats in a number of ways. One general approach may be to simply not engage. This Luddite approach, though, comes with a fairly high cost given the importance of staying up with technological capabilities in most fields. Another may be to engage minimally so as to minimize a sense of threats. This approach does not require sophisticated cybersecurity defense skills, but this is about a kind of “security through obscurity” (in which the user himself or herself is obscured or hidden…in this case through non-engagement). Along this continuum are increasing levels of engagement (Figure 1). This continuum does not address the potential deployment of cybersecurity measures or countermeasures.

Figure 1. Engagement levels in cyberspace (a continuum)

Even non-engagement does not mean there is no effect of cybersecurity lapses. After all, people in modern societies are still reliant on public works, electric grids, modern banking, online news, weather modeling, law enforcement, national defense, and pretty much various systems dependent on cyber. Post Stuxnet and its follow-on technologies, there have been more public awareness of the vulnerabilities of SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) systems. Cyberattacks on physical systems may have devastating effects (Bhalodia, Zala, & Nandy, 2017).

Hard-Wired Cognitive Limits

Whatever knowledge individuals may bring to the cybersecurity challenge, they do come at the challenge with challenges. For example, people tend to have a “confirmation bias,” which means that when they observe new information, they tend to try to fit that into a pre-existing conceptualization. If they observe something that goes against an earlier conceptualization, they will actually attempt to test their hypothesis with a “positive test strategy” instead of looking for ways to refute their hypothesis (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 80 - 81). Confirmation bias can close off accurate engagement with the world because each person is only seeking to reinforce what they already think they know.

Another cognitive bias is termed “WYSIATI” or “what you see is all there is” (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 85 – 88). This theory suggests that people do not consider “known unknowns” or “unknown unknowns” when making decisions but only consider what they have seen, which is also cognitively limiting. Based on the “law of small numbers,” people tend to over-weight observations even when they are limited and statistically insignificant (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 112 – 118). With necessary skepticism, the work would benefit from larger samples to increase the power of the research and to raise the confidence level of the findings. Another common cognitive bias is “availability bias.”

Here people tend to imagine that certain events are more likely than others because examples of that type of event come to mind more readily (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 138 – 145). Here, salience of memory is conflated with higher probabilities of occurrence. In terms of rationality in decision-making, people may be thrown off rational decision-making by a host of factors. They can subconsciously anchor to a certain number mentioned first. They are sensitive to how a context is framed or contextualized (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 371 – 374). They tend to be loss averse and will make irrational choices to prevent against loss (Kahneman, 2011, pp. 283 – 288). Beyond cognitive biases, there are challenges with executive control and attentional focus. Many lack the self-regulation skills to control their own behaviors.

These cognitive limits are not necessarily mitigated when people are engaging in a group context. In groups, people tend to follow authority figures in “obedience to authority” dynamics (Milgram, 1963). They have a tendency to experience a dissipation of individual responsibility and apathy in the presence of a group (“bystander effect,” “diffusion of responsibility”) (Darley & Latané, 1968). In group decision-making, people tend towards “groupthink” (Janis, 1972). A version of groupthink is the “Abilene paradox,” based on unthinking acceptance of an initial suggestion (based in part on social conformity) and not considering actual interests (Harvey, 1996) and impacts of the decision. Cultural factors may affect the group members’ “habits of thought” and so limit potentially creative approaches to problem-solving.

And yet, people do by necessity have to collaborate to achieve any number of tasks. There are some problems for which the “wisdom of crowds” may be harnessed:

…under the right circumstances, groups are remarkably intelligent, and are often smarter than the smartest people in them. Groups do not need to be dominated by exceptionally intelligent people in order to be smart. Even if most of the people within a group are not especially well-informed or rational, it can still reach a collectively wise decision (Surowiecki, 2004, pp. xiii – xiv)

James Surowiecki (2004) suggests that groups of common folk with individual imperfect judgments can be aggregated “under the right circumstances” in a way that makes for effective decision-making. The right circumstances include the following three types of problems:

  • 1. Cognition problems “that have or will have definite solutions” (p. xvii),
  • 2. Coordination problems that require members of a group to coordinate with each other (pp. xvii – xviii), and
  • 3. Cooperation problems that “involve the challenge of getting self-interested, distrustful people to work together, even when narrow self-interest would seem to dictate that no individual should take part.” (p. xviii).

It does not seem to be a wide stretch to see any of the above three problem types as applicable in a cybersecurity context and ripe for solving with a mass mind, even an electronic hive mind. How individual and human cognition manifest in a hive mind context is generally unexplored at present. In cyber psychology, online behavior has been studied through an evolutionary frame in terms of four domains: “(1) mating and sexual competition, (2) parenting and kinship, (3) trust and social exchange, and (4) personal information management” (Piazza & Bering, 2009, p. 1258). This work takes a different tact by looking at a specific type of “hive mind” (as a framework) surrounding cybersecurity, a form of defense.

EXPLORING THE ELECTRONIC HIVE MIND RE: CYBERSECURITY

One of the core challenges in this chapter is to define the electronic hive mind regarding cybersecurity. As noted earlier, the focus is on the non-cybersecurity expert parts of the hive mind in order to understand what is understood among the more general population. The three general research areas explored are as follows:

  • 1. What is the level of sophistication of the electronic hive mind in regards to cybersecurity? Are there blind spots (lacunae) regarding cybersecurity? If so, what are these, are they from critical areas of cybersecurity, and why might these exist?
  • 2. How does the folk electronic hive mind differ from the expressions of cybersecurity experts on the Social Web / Web 2.0? If these exist, what are the main differences, and why might these exist?
  • 3. Is the “hive mind” (related to cybersecurity) more reflective of (a) a mob mentality or herd mind, or is it more reflective of (b) collective intelligence and “wisdom of crowds”? Is the hive mind functioning effectively and prosocially regarding cybersecurity (or not)? How so? How not?

To capture a sense of this hive mind, the following online data sources were used:

  • • Text-based Data
    • o Web Search (Google Search, Google Correlate)
    • o Social News Sharing (Reddit)
    • o Word Uses in Scans of Masses of Books (Google Books Ngram Viewer)
    • o #networks and Messages (Twitter) (using NodeXL and NVivo 11 Plus)
  • • Social Imagery (Google Images, Flickr)
    • o Related Tags Nsetworks (abstraction, meta) (Flickr)
  • • Audio Files (iTunes)
  • • Social Videos (YouTube)
  • • Slideshows (SlideShare)

Micro, Meso, and Macro Levels of the Hive Mind

The sources range from the micro to the meso to the macro levels. At the micro level, researchers have a zoomed-in proximal view of a single node in the hive and the perspectives of that individual and his / her consciousness regarding the topic. The details at the micro-level are specific to the code. Much of this level exists in private groups and denied spaces. At the meso level, there are smaller groups of shared consciousness. These are groups of experts who specialize in particular professional niches. Membership is determined by talent and capabilities and trustworthiness.

At the macro level, this is the proverbial 30,000-foot distal level with more summary and abstract data (which tells more coarse-grained and vague narratives). This is conceptualized as the broad public parts of the electronic hive mind. Said another way, the ability to receive information depends on how prepared the individual or group or population is to that information. At worst, people may misapprehend (misunderstand). Second worse would be if they do not comprehend at all and at least realize that.

TEXT-BASED DATA

The Electronic Hive Mind in Web-Based Search

When conducting Web searches, at least in initial years, people may have thought that their searches were private and maybe anonymized. After all, they were in the privacy of their own comfortable home and other spaces. It turns out that such data have been logged from the beginning by most service providers. In exploring such data, data scientists found the information could be reverse-engineered back to a specific individual with fairly high accuracy. In the interests of protecting user privacy, large search companies have decided against releasing individual search data for research but have enabled access at macro population-scale level. These data enable a glimpse at the changing macro patterns of people’s interests and information exploration over extended time. One inference from these time-based associations is that in-world incidences are informing the searches, given how people often search “just in time” for information that they need.

Google Correlate is an online tool that enables access to Google Search terms whose time-based search patterns correlate with that of the target term over time (from 2004 to the present in 2017, for a 13-year span) (FAQ – Google Correlate, 2007). One query that would be potentially useful in this context is to run “cyber” as the target search term and to see if any of the top 20 correlated search terms reflect cybersecurity or a similar term. In other words, when cyber is being explored, is security also top-of-mind? These queries are available for over 50 countries. The results are shown in a line graph, with time on the x-axis and the normalized search activity (standard deviations above the mean for the search term at that particular time) on the y-axis. (See Figure 2.)

Figure 2. “Cyber” and “cyber Monday” (r=0.9980) in the U.S.

The correlated terms are listed in descending order on the site (Figure 3). In expanded view, some 20 top correlations are shown. In cases where there are no correlates that is indicated as well. The time-series relationships can be seen quite effectively in the linegraph.

Figure 3. “Cyber” and top 20 Google search term correlations in Australia (in Google Correlate)

In same-day queries of over 50 different countries to see what the associations were for “cyber,” only in one country was there a word related to “cybersecurity.” In the Philippines, the top correlation with “cyber” as a search term is “cyber crime.” [To accommodate for the range of the world’s languages expressed with UTF-8, Google Translate was used to render the terms readable to the author.] In no other country was any other term that could be remotely tied to cybersecurity associated with the “cyber” search in Google Search. For many of the countries, “cyber” was related to sales and sales events (think “cyber monday”). [The actual data is downloadable in .csv format courtesy of Google Correlate.]

The Electronic Hive Mind in Social News Sharing

Interestingly, the news-sharing bulletin board Reddit has been referred to as a social technology that enables the collective “hive mind” albeit in a slightly pejorative sense. Reddit (as in “read it”) enables members to vote up or vote down a reference to an online published news source. (Search engines offer an “upvote” and “downvote” function, too, based on the search algorithms and the results that they return to particular text-based queries. The algorithms are designed to not only particularize findings based on understood searcher intent but also on the popularity and quality of the returned sites.) Popular works attain more attention because of their placement on the website’s front page, and less popular works have even less opportunity to attract an audience from the site’s users / readers. [This aligns with the Matthew effect, found in online social sharing sites, where the few attain most of the attention, and the majority of contributors are in the “long tail” of a power law curve with little to no attention.

This concept is drawn from Matthew 25:14-25:30, in the parable of the talents. In the Bible, Matthew 25:29 reads: “For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath,” in reference to money invested appropriately.] Here, the editor role is fulfilled by group members. Their ability to vote is an expression of democracy-in-action and egalitarianism (one person, one vote—per posting). One researcher writes:

When such a post appears on reddit’s front page it has effectively been endorsed by the community (through the voting system) and broadcast to all of the community’s members who visit reddit while the post is visible on the front page. Do these successful ‘meta’ posts influence the collective behaviour of the website’s users? If they do, then this would constitute evidence that the voting system allows the community to self-regulate at a high level. If they do not, this suggests that the hive mind suffers from cognitive dissonance or poor discipline/memory. (Mills, 2011, p. 11)

This researcher found that on Reddit that “minority opinions are found to be slightly marginalised (sic) but not excluded from high visibility locations (Mills, 2011, p. 1). The concern is that collaborative systems may lead to unthinking or unexamined consensus instead of offering valuable human filtering of news to control for information overload. Other researchers express concern that online communities like Reddit may potentially lead to heightened tensions and discrimination between groups and even less democracy based on the depersonalization of other (Workman, 2014, p. 13).

To better understand the electronic hive mind, the main message headings were scraped from three subreddits, two for general users, and one specifically identified for cybersecurity professionals. A screenshot of the “cybersecurity” subreddit (https://www.reddit.com/r/cybersecurity/) is available in Figure 5. At the time of the data capture, the subreddit had 10.974 readers, and 48 users were online at that time. This is a moderated subreddit, with the moderators listed by their handles: Chumstick, CDSEChris, Jess_V, Spncrgmn.

THE ELECTRONIC HIVE MIND IN MASS-SCALE SCANNED BOOKS

The Google Books Ngram Viewer, aptly named a “language time machine” (Weingarten, Sept. 9, 2013), enables users to explore word, phrase, name, and number histories in terms of their usages in published books, from the 1500s to 2000 or so, based on various text corpora in different languages. As a non-consumptive tool, it does not allow access to the underlying data, but it does offer word frequency counts above a word count threshold to show the commonality of term usages over time. “Cyber” and “cybersecurity” were both run together in the Google Books Ngram Viewer from 1950 to 2000, and based on the English corpus. The results may be seen in Figure 10, and it is clear that the popularity of “cyber” has far outpaced the reference to “cybersecurity.” The lines on the linegraph are not dispositive, but they do suggest greater awareness and usage of “cyber” as compared to “cybersecurity.”

Figure 10. “Cyber” and “cybersecurity” from 1950-2000 in Google Books Ngram Viewer

The Electronic Hive Mind in #Hashtag Networks

Another way to get at a part of the electronic hive mind on cybersecurity involves exploring the hashtag network from the network of communicators discussing #cybersecurity on the Twitter microblogging site. This extraction from the Twitter API, using the Network Overview, Discovery and Exploration for Excel (NodeXL) add-on to Excel resulted in a network graph with 527 vertices (nodes) and 629 unique edges (links). There were 155 self-loops in the relationships (user accounts that self-retweeted or which self-replied). Over all, there were 896 relationships in this network. The network graph diameter was nine (9), and the average geodesic distance was 4.19.

In this hashtag network, there were 133 groups or clusters (as extracted using the Clauset-Newman-Moore algorithm), and some smaller motifs. [The parameter settings on NodeXL was for the capture of a basic #hashtag network without the inclusion of the communicators’ friends, with a limit of 18,000 Tweets limited by NodeXL, beyond the rate-limits of the Twitter API). Figure 11 shows the various groups and “motifs” discussing this topic at the time of the data capture.

Figure 11. #cybersecurity hashtag network on Twitter (with 527 vertices and 629 unique edges)

In Figure 12, these show the most commonly mentioned words and hashtags in the discussions around cybersecurity. This word cloud provides auto-extracted summary data about the discussions.
